results.finding: Catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus is recommended for symptomatic, recurrent episodes of typical (CTI-dependent) flutter, and should be considered after the first symptomatic episode.
results.source: Brugada J et al., 2019 ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with supraventricular tachycardia. Eur Heart J 2020;41:655-720

results.finding: Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs should not be used in atrial flutter without AV-nodal blockade, because slowing the flutter cycle can produce 1:1 conduction.

results.finding: Oral anticoagulation, preferably a direct oral anticoagulant, is recommended for patients with a CHA2DS2-VA score of 2 or more; the same thromboembolic risk assessment applies to atrial flutter.

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction can switch to 1:1 conduction at about 300 bpm, often with aberrant wide QRS, and cause syncope
A normal-rate resting ECG does not exclude paroxysmal atrial flutter
Class IC drugs slow the flutter rate and can permit 1:1 conduction unless an AV-nodal blocker is given
Anticoagulation in atrial flutter follows CHA2DS2-VA as in atrial fibrillation (ESC 2024)
Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is the definitive therapy for typical flutter

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Caldwell is a 67-year-old Caucasian male with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes (diet-controlled), and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department by ambulance after a single episode of transient loss of consciousness. His neighbor, who had stopped by for a visit, reports that the patient was standing at his kitchen counter when he suddenly collapsed without any prodromal warning, falling forward and catching himself partially on the countertop. He was unresponsive for an estimated 10 to 15 seconds, then regained consciousness spontaneously and immediately asked what had happened. There was no convulsive activity, no tonic stiffening, no rhythmic jerking, no tongue biting, and no urinary incontinence. Recovery was described as immediate and complete — he was coherent and conversational within 30 seconds. The neighbor noted that just before the event the patient had commented he felt his heart 'racing' for a few seconds. He endorses approximately three months of episodic palpitations that he describes as a rapid fluttering sensation in his chest, generally lasting 10 to 30 minutes and resolving on their own. His primary care physician evaluated him for these episodes eight weeks ago. An ECG performed in the office at that visit showed a rate of 88 bpm with a regular rhythm and was documented as 'sinus rhythm, normal.' He was reassured that the palpitations were likely related to anxiety given an ongoing stressful period following retirement, and no further workup was arranged at that time. He has not been started on any new medications. He denies chest pain, dyspnea at rest, exertional pre-syncope, fever, recent illness, or ingestion of stimulants or new supplements. He has had no prior syncopal episodes. On review of systems, he endorses fatigue for the past two to three months and mild exertional dyspnea when climbing stairs, which he attributed to deconditioning.
